summary: Defines a service for locating Public Key Infrastructure repositories using DNS SRV records, per RFC 2782. This lets systems that use certificates find where certificates are kept. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4386 defines a way for a program that needs a certificate to find out where the certificates for a domain are kept. It uses a DNS record of the SRV kind, under the fixed name _PKIXREP, with the protocol spelled out in the name. The client asks DNS, gets the host and port of the repository, and then fetches the certificate over that protocol.

questions: how to locate a pki repository with dns srv
how to locate a pki repository with dns
what is the pkix repository locator service
how do certificate clients find a repository
subtitle: How a certificate-using program can find a domain's PKI repository by asking DNS for an SRV record.

tldr.problem: The RFCs that define how to fetch certificates and revocation information all assume the client already knows which repository to use and how to reach it, and the existing ways of publishing that information are tied to one protocol each.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines an SRV record for a repository locator service, with the service label _PKIXREP and a protocol label for each access method, so a client asks DNS for _PKIXREP._LDAP.example.com and is told the host and port of the repository to query.
tldr.outcome: The approach is aimed at environments where only a domain name is available; where a certificate already carries the information, no lookup is needed. It is an Experimental specification.

today: RFC 4386 is an Experimental document published in February 2006. It was later updated by RFC 8553, which fixes specifications that use underscored node names in DNS records.

sections.title: Why a Repository Locator Service
sections.content:
A number of RFCs, among them the operational protocols for LDAP, OCSP and for FTP and HTTP, have specified operational protocols for retrieving PKI data, including public-key certificates and revocation information, from PKI repositories. Those documents assume that a certificate-using system already has the information necessary to identify, locate and connect to the PKI repository with a specific protocol.

Some tools are available in protocol-specific environments for this purpose, such as knowledge references in directory systems, but they are restricted to use with a single protocol and do not share a common means of publication. This document provides a solution through the use of Service Record resource records in DNS. The solution is expected to be particularly useful in environments where only a domain name is available; in other situations, for example where a certificate is available that already contains the required information, such a DNS lookup is not needed.

RFC 2782 defines the DNS record for specifying the location of services. This document defines SRV records for a PKI repository locator service, so that PKI clients can obtain the information they need to connect to a domain's PKI repository, including which protocols that domain supports for access to its repository.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocols that fetch certificates are already written. What they leave out is how a program finds the server to fetch from. The memo puts that answer in DNS, where a domain name is usually all a client has to go on.

sections.title: The SRV Record Definition
sections.content:
The format of the SRV record, whose DNS type code is 33, is _Service._Proto.Name TTL Class SRV Priority Weight Port Target. For the PKI repository locator service the symbolic name is PKIXREP, and when it is used in an SRV record this name must be prepended with an underscore character.

The protocols that can be included in PKIXREP SRV records are LDAP with the prefix _LDAP, HTTP with the prefix _HTTP, and OCSP with the prefix _OCSP. Assignments of protocol prefixes for new PKI repository protocols should be defined in the document that specifies the protocol.

The existence of multiple repositories may be determined by making separate DNS queries for each of the protocols supported by the client. If that turns out to be unacceptably inefficient because of a proliferation of repository protocols at some future date, the memo suggests the service discovery protocol could be extended to let a repository advertise the protocols it supports.
sections.plainLanguage: The name of the record says two things: that it points at a certificate repository, and which protocol to speak to it. A client that speaks LDAP looks for one name, and a client that speaks HTTP looks for another.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The example uses the fictional domain example.com to show how a certificate-using system uses the records. Alice is an email client that needs a certificate for a recipient, and her client system supports LDAP for certificate retrieval. The recipient is Bob, whose email address is bob@example.com, and example.test maintains a border directory PKI repository from which Bob's certificate is available over LDAP at border.example.com.

Alice's client system retrieves, via DNS, the SRV record for _PKIXREP._LDAP.example.com. The QNAME of the DNS query is _PKIXREP._LDAP.example.com, the QCLASS is IN, and the QTYPE is SRV. The result should include the host address for example.com's border directory system.

If example.com operated its service on a number of hosts, more than one SRV record would be returned, and RFC 2782 defines the procedure for deciding which of them should be accessed first.
sections.plainLanguage: The client's mail program needs a certificate for a recipient and knows how to fetch certificates over LDAP but not where they are kept. It asks DNS for the name that combines the two, and DNS answers with the machine that holds them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security issues regarding the PKI repositories themselves are outside the scope of this document; for LDAP repositories, for example, the specific security considerations are addressed in RFC 2559. Security issues with respect to the use of SRV records in general are addressed in RFC 2782, and those issues apply to the use of SRV records in the context of the PKIXREP service defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not add security of its own. It points at the documents that cover the repository and the DNS record, and says their warnings apply here too.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document reserves the use of the _PKIXREP service label. Since the service may pass messages over a number of different transports, each message must be associated with a specific transport, and to keep the association between _PKIXREP and the underlying services deterministic, IANA created a new registry, PKIX SRV Protocol Labels. An entry in that registry consists of a label name and a pointer to a specification describing how the protocol named in the label uses SRV. Specifications should conform to the requirements listed in RFC 2434 for specification required.
sections.plainLanguage: The label _PKIXREP is reserved, and the protocols that may appear under it are listed in a registry so that each one always means the same thing.

viz.caption: WHAT THE MEMO ADDS TO THE EXISTING PKI PROTOCOLS

items.title: Retrieval protocols exist
items.text: RFCs already define how to fetch certificates and revocation data over LDAP, HTTP or OCSP.

items.title: The gap they leave
items.text: Those documents assume the client already knows which repository to use and how to reach it.

items.title: The fix
items.text: Publish the repository in DNS as an SRV record under a fixed service label.

viz.caption: THE SRV RECORD FORMAT AND THE PROTOCOL PREFIXES

data.title: PKIXREP SRV records
data.code:
_Service._Proto.Name TTL Class SRV Priority Weight Port Target

Protocol     SRV Prefix

LDAP         _LDAP
HTTP         _HTTP
OCSP         _OCSP
